title: Cap. XII: If Adam's sin is not imputed, why Christ's merits? — Confession XI
pass_a_gloss: The rest I pass by—bare affirmations without reason: I will only add this, which both wears some appearance of an argument and shows how far those who accuse us recede from our public Confession of faith and approach Pighianism. If, he says, the first parent's sin is not imputed, what need is there of the imputation of Christ's merits? If he meant either original sin or mediate imputation, he would say nothing contrary to the cause we plead; he would only say something false and unworthy of a theologian, not to say of a Christian. For we need the imputation of Christ's righteousness so that we may also be justified from our other sins, which are all too many: but when he means Adam's actual sin and its immediate imputation, who does not see that the guilt of original sin is denied by him? And that that sin, as far as condemnation or justification is concerned, is held for nothing? It is enough, he adds, [to have] sanctification which takes away that disease. Is it then, I ask, a disease such that it is not sin? such that it does not condemn? Compare, I beg, with such men's doctrine article XI of the Confession of faith: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes all and every human being—not even little ones still hiding in their mothers' wombs excepted—guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin as regards blame, although those who are sons of God are by no means therefore condemned, because God of his free goodness and mercy does not impute it to them. We say besides that this perversity always brings forth some fruits of malice and rebellion, and so on.
pass_b_english: I leave the rest—bare assertions without reason—and add only this, which both looks like an argument and shows how far our accusers leave our public Confession and drift toward Pighianism. If, he says, the first parent's sin is not imputed, why impute Christ's merits? Had he meant original sin or mediate imputation, he would not contradict our cause; he would only say something false and unfit for a theologian, let alone a Christian. We need Christ's righteousness imputed so we may also be justified from our many other sins. But when he means Adam's actual sin and its immediate imputation, who does not see that he denies original sin's guilt, and treats that sin as nothing for condemnation or justification? Sanctification that removes the disease is enough, he adds. Is it then a disease that is not sin, that does not condemn? Set that teaching beside Confession article XI: we believe this vice is truly sin, which makes every human being—even infants still in the womb—liable to eternal death before God. We also affirm that even after baptism it remains truly sin as to blame, though the sons of God are not therefore condemned, because God of free goodness and mercy does not impute it to them. We add that this perversity always bears some fruits of malice and rebellion.
source_text: Caetera praetermitto, nudas sine ratione affirmationes: illud tantum subiungam, quod & speciem aliquam prae se fert argumenti, & quam a publica fidei nostrae Confessione recedant & ad Pighianismum accedant illi qui nos accusant, prodit. Si peccatum, inquit, primi parentis non imputatur, quid opus imputatione meritorum Christi? Si vel peccatum originale intelligeret, vel imputationem mediatam, nihil diceret causae, quam agimus repugnans, diceret tantum aliquid falsum, & Theologo indignum, ne dicam Christiano. Opus enim nobis est imputatione justitiae Christi, ut etiam ab aliis peccatis nostris, quae nimium multa sunt, justificemur: Sed cum peccatum actuale Adami intelligat, illiusque imputationem immediatam, quis non videt ab eo peccati originalis reatum negari? Idque peccatum, quantum ad condemnationem vel justificationem attinet, pro nullo haberi? Sufficit, addit, sanctificatio quae tollat illum morbum. Est-ne igitur, inquam, ita morbus ut non sit peccatum? ut non damnet? Confer quaeso cum hujusmodi hominum doctrina articulum XI. Confessionis fidei; Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet, quamvis qui filii Dei sunt, minime idcirco condemnentur, quoniam videlicet Deus pro gratuita sua bonitate & misericordia illud ipsis non imputat. Dicimus praeterea hanc perversitatem semper edere fructus aliquos malitiae & rebellionis, &c.
